I've ended the session; the work itself was done. Before answering your four points, I measured that session's cost, because it changes the answer to your model question.

**What narration actually cost.** That session made 22 calls to the coding model: 11 to do the work and 11 *only* to narrate. Each call re-reads the whole conversation, about 276k tokens here, because this conversation is very long. So narration roughly doubled the cost. Almost all of it came from those extra calls; the narration words themselves were a tiny share. In a fresh session the conversation would be much smaller, but the doubling would remain.

That means **switching the narration to Haiku only saves money if the coding model stops making those calls.** Today it writes every narration itself, through the `narrate` tool, so there's no separate narration model to swap yet. That's the big question, Q4.

---

❓ **Q1** - **Words appear while you talk.** While recording, the extension re-transcribes what you've said so far about once a second and shows it greyed out in the box. When you stop, a final pass replaces it, and you check and press Enter as now. That's cheap on your GPU; without a GPU it updates more slowly.

➡️ Yes, live words about once a second.

---

❓ **Q2** - **Fixed controls.** Move Sample voices, Settings and Transcript out of the scrolling captions into the fixed bar at the top, as small icons with tooltips (voice, gear, document), to the right of Pause / Skip / Mute.

➡️ Yes.

---

❓ **Q3** - **A more modern look.** Rather than guess at "modern", I'll build a page with 3 clearly different directions for the panel, using the same content and states. You pick one at a browser link, as you did with the icons. Colours keep their meanings throughout: amber pause, green resume, red muted.

➡️ Yes, a catalog of 3 directions.

---

❓ **Q4** - **Who writes the narration?** Three options:
- **(a) Same as today, but fewer calls.** The coding model narrates in the same call as its edits instead of in separate calls. This roughly halves the extra cost with no new parts, but the narration is still written by the expensive model.
- **(b) A separate narrator model, Haiku by default and set in the settings file.** The coding model just works, with no narration calls and no session script in its context. Haiku watches what it does: every edit and command, plus the coding model's own messages. Haiku writes the narration, points at the code, and answers your simple questions. The voice still holds the coding model before each edit until the narration has been said, so the pacing stays.

  Costs of (b):
  - It's the biggest rebuild so far.
  - Haiku only knows the "why" from what the coding model writes and does, so explanations may be shallower.

- **(c) Both.** Ship (a) now for a quick win, then design (b) properly in its own session.

- **Fewer narration calls.** The agent now narrates in the same call as the edit it describes, which should remove most of the narration-only calls that doubled the cost. I'll measure it on your next session.

## Narrator and coder: what I'd do

Your instinct is right: **narrating and coding should be separate jobs, run by an orchestrator.** The last session showed why. Half of the coding model's calls were narration only. Carrying all the narration rules also competes with the coding: I broke one of them myself by sending two narrations at once.

**Will Haiku understand what's going on?** It doesn't need to search the code the way the coder does, because its job is explaining decisions, not making them. It would see:
- every edit exactly (before and after)
- the files the coder read
- the output of each command
- everything the coder writes along the way, such as "I'll put the check here because…"

That covers most of what a senior engineer says out loud. What it can't see is reasoning the coder never writes down. Two ways around that:
- **A short "why" per change.** The coder writes one line of why before each change: ordinary text, no extra call.
- **Hand the hard questions to the coder.** When you ask a deep "why" that the narrator can't answer, it passes the question to the coder, so the expensive model is used only when it's needed.

The narrator model would be a setting: Haiku by default, Sonnet if Haiku is too shallow, or the same model as the coder.

**Where the orchestrator lives.** There are two options:
- **(i) Inside the agent you already use, via its hooks.** Before each edit, a hook asks the narrator to explain it, waits for the voice, then lets the edit through. Your corrections reach the coder as the reason a step was held back. You keep working in your normal Claude Code chat, but it needs one adapter per agent: Claude Code hooks, an OpenCode plugin.
- **(ii) Our own program running the coder in the background, next to the narrator.** It gives full control and the cleanest separation, but sessions would no longer happen in your normal chat. I'd also need to check whether it can use your Claude subscription or needs an API key, which matters for work billing.

➡️ My recommendation is **(i)**, but first a cheap experiment to settle your doubt. I'd replay the last session's real edits and messages to Haiku and put its narration next to what the coder actually said, side by side with audio, at a browser link. If Haiku is good enough, we design (i) properly in its own session, with a decision record that replaces decision 0004 (agent-agnostic).

Two jobs, then: build design B into the real panel, and run the Haiku experiment, judging its accuracy myself. First I'll check how this machine can reach Haiku.
